paras: The lynching of Hicks Ross was the reported hanging of a Black prisoner by a mob that took him from the jail at Linden, Cass County, Texas, on Sunday, July 10, 1881. He had been jailed on the accusation of fatally cutting Dr. H. J. Avinger, a physician at Avinger Station on the East Line railroad. Word of the lynching came through the Dallas Herald, first as a rumor 'pretty well confirmed' and then as beyond 'little doubt'.

According to the Milan Exchange, Dr. Avinger 'engaged in a row' with a Black man at Avinger Station on Saturday, June 25, and was slashed across the bowels with a razor. The Memphis Appeal named the man as Hicks Ross, said he used a knife, and reported that he was arrested and confined in Linden jail. The doctor died on June 30, and a post mortem found two intestines cut and gangrene.

The Dallas Herald, citing 'accounts of the affair', called the killing 'an unprovoked and most malicious murder' and complained that the accused had been granted bail of $2,500. He had not been able to give that bail and remained in jail.

A special dispatch from Marshall dated July 12 reported that the man who killed the doctor had been taken from the jail by a mob on Sunday and hanged. The correspondent wrote that the rumor was confirmed by telegraph dispatches and that, since the Linden jail was 'one of the strongest in the state', great violence must have been used. The dispatch gave no account of the mob's size, the hour, or where the man was hanged.

On July 15 the Dallas Herald wrote that there seemed 'little doubt of the lynching' and explained that public sentiment against the prisoner was too strong to await the law. No report of an inquest, arrests of mob members, or other official response appears in the coverage.

Coverage was brief and regional, carried in Texas news columns rather than as telegraph headlines. Before the lynching, the Memphis Appeal and the Milan Exchange in Tennessee ran short items on the wounding, and the Dallas Herald noted the doctor's death. The lynching itself appeared in the Dallas Herald's daily and weekly editions, in the Marshall dispatch of July 13 and 14 and in a paragraph on July 15 that the weekly reprinted on July 21.

The Herald treated the prisoner's guilt as settled, calling him 'the negro who murdered Dr. H. J. Avinger' and the act a 'heinous deed'. It presented the lynching as the result of public impatience with 'the slow process of the law, with its delays and uncertainties', without criticism of the mob.

Accounts of the original wounding differ: the Milan Exchange described a 'row' between the two men, while the Dallas Herald called it unprovoked. The Memphis Appeal said the weapon was a knife and the Milan Exchange a razor, and none of these reports was from a local paper.

reader.title: Lynching of Hicks Ross
bases: A Marshall dispatch reported that a Black man jailed at Linden on a murder accusation was taken from the jail by a mob and hanged, and the Dallas Herald called it a lynching (A5, A6).

The only reports, in the Dallas Herald, say a mob took the jailed man from Linden jail and hanged him because public sentiment would not await the law (A5, A6), but they present it as rumor 'pretty well confirmed' and 'little doubt', with no local account, so the killing rests on secondhand report.

The wounding and the arrest are reported by three papers (A1, A2, A3), but the seizure and hanging appear only in the Dallas Herald, in one Marshall dispatch (A4, A5) and the paper's own follow-up paragraph (A6, reprinted A7).
